Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 63, verse 1:

Surah al-Munafiqun

It is Medinan, and its number of verses is eleven, without disagreement. Its connection (wajh al-ittisal) to the previous surah is that Surah al-Jumu'ah mentioned the believers, while this one mentions their opposites, the hypocrites (al-munafiqun). For this reason Sa'id ibn Mansur and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat related with a good chain (bi-sanad hasan) from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite in the Friday prayer Surah al-Jumu'ah, thereby urging the believers on, and in the second rak'ah Surah al-Munafiqun, thereby rebuking the hypocrites." Abu Hayyan said regarding this: since the cause of dispersing from listening to the sermon was often from the hypocrites, and many of the believers followed them in that because of their joy at the caravan that had arrived with provisions, at a time of famine, [the surah] mentioned the hypocrites, what they were upon of hatred for the people of faith, and followed with the ugliness of their deeds and their statements. The first explanation is better.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿When the hypocrites come to you﴾ meaning they attend your assembly. The intended ones are Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his companions. ﴿They say: "We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah."﴾ The emphasis by "inna" and the lam serves to affirm the content of the statement, which is their knowledge of this proposition that is testified to, and so it conveys the emphasis of the testimony, and indicates that they claim in it agreement of the tongue with the heart, though in itself it may fall upon truth or falsehood. The emphasis in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger﴾ is for greater care regarding the matter of the statement in reality, or it is merely to match their practice. The sentence is inserted parenthetically to remove what might be suspected from His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are indeed liars﴾, namely that the denial returns to the very content of the testified statement from the outset. Al-Tibi mentioned that this is a type of completion (tatmim) of subtle method, and its parallel is the saying of Abu al-Tayyib:

"And you despise the world with the contempt of one who has tried it, you see all that is in it, and far be you from being perishing."

So the denial returns to "nashhadu" in terms of the implicit statement indicated by the emphasis, which is the claim of agreement in the testimony, meaning: "And Allah bears witness that they are indeed liars in what they implied in their statement 'we bear witness' of claiming agreement of tongue and heart in this testimony." It may be said: testimony is a specific kind of statement, namely that in which the tongue agrees with the heart; the testimony of falsehood, however, is used figuratively, like applying the term "sale" to what is not valid. So they are liars in their saying "we bear witness", which is based on calling their saying a testimony, and this is what is meant by the one who said: that is, they are liars in calling that a testimony. So reflect well.

On this basis, establishing their lying does not require their claim of agreement to be implied, because the word is laid down for the one who agrees. It is also permitted that the denial returns to their statement ﴿that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah﴾ in terms of the necessary implication of the content of the statement, which amounts to its returning to the implicit statement; and that it returns to it in terms of what is in their minds, meaning: they are liars in their statement ﴿that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah﴾ in their own estimation, because they believed it to be false and a statement contrary to the actual state of the one spoken of. It was said: on this basis the lying is the legal kind, to which blame attaches; do you not see that mujtahids are not described as liars, though they may be described as mistaken?

Al-Allamah al-Thani permitted that the denial returns to the oaths of the hypocrites, and they claimed that they did not say ﴿Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse from around him﴾ and ﴿If we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel the meaner therefrom﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 7, 8], based on what is related in Sahih al-Bukhari: "From Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: I was on an expedition with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and I heard Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul say: 'Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse from around him, and if we return from his presence, the mightier will surely expel the meaner therefrom.' So I mentioned that to my uncle, and he mentioned it to the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ), and he summoned me, and I related it to him. The Messenger of Allah (upon him be prayers and peace) sent to Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his companions, and they swore that they had not said it. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) denied me and confirmed him, and a grief came upon me such as had never befallen me before. I sat in the house, and my uncle said to me: 'You did not intend except that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would deny you and be displeased with you.' Then Allah revealed ﴿When the hypocrites come to you﴾, and the Prophet (ﷺ) sent for me, recited it, and said: 'Indeed Allah has confirmed you, O Zayd.'"

Some eminent scholars permitted that the meaning is: the hypocrites' nature is lying, even if they speak truly in this report. Whichever is the case, the Nazzam's inference from the verse is not complete, namely that the truth of a report is its conformity to the belief of the one reporting, even if that belief is mistaken, and its falsehood is its non-conformity. The manifestation of "the hypocrites" in the place of the pronoun serves to censure them and to indicate the reason for the ruling. The discussion regarding "idha" is as has passed just now.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 63, verse 2:

﴿They took their oaths﴾, that is, the false ones, as indicated by the genitive construction. ﴿As a shield﴾, that is, a protection against what is directed at them of punishment by killing, or captivity, or otherwise. Qatadah said: "Whenever something of theirs appeared that would bring them punishment, they swore falsely to protect their property and their blood." This is an independent statement, enumerating their vices and that it was their custom to seek cover (istijnan) behind false oaths, just as they sought cover behind false testimony. It is also permissible that by "their oaths" is meant their earlier testimony. The Arabs treated testimony (shahadah) and verbs of knowledge and certainty as oaths, and they followed them with what follows an oath, and used them to confirm speech as an oath is used to confirm it. For this reason the word "oath" (yamin) is applied to them. Abu Hanifah cited this as evidence that "I testify" (ashhadu) is an oath. Ibn al-Munir objected to this, saying that the most the verse shows is that it is called an oath, whereas the question is whether expiation (kaffarah) is obligatory on account of it, not whether the name applies. Not everything called an oath entails expiation: if one says "I swear (uhlifu) to such-and-such," expiation is not obligatory on him, even though it is an oath. The plural is used in view of the multiplicity of speakers. This statement, according to this reading, is a resumption (isti'naf) that explains the purpose of their saying that, together with the severe censure expressed by what follows it. It was also said that ﴿they took﴾ (ittakhadhu) is the apodosis (jawab) of "when" (idha), and the clause ﴿they said﴾ (qalu) preceding it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), with qad either implied or not. This is contrary to the apparent meaning, and further from it is making the clause a circumstantial clause while supposing an apodosis for idha. Al-Dahhak said: that is, they took their oath by God that they were truly of you as a shield against being killed, or taken captive, or something similar to what the unbelievers do to them. From this the poet took his words:

"They claimed Islam only to preserve their blood,
lest they be ..."

It is also reported from al-Suddi that they took this as a shield against the prayer being performed over them when they died. This, as you see, is far-fetched, and so is what precedes it.

﴿So they barred [others] from the way of God﴾, that is, whoever wished to enter the religion of Islam, or whoever wished to perform any act of obedience, taking the verb as transitive with the object omitted; or they turned away from Islam in actuality, taking the verb as intransitive. Whichever it is, the meaning, as has been said, is that they persisted in this. Some eminent scholars took the oaths to include what was reported of them concerning testimony. Then he said: taking them as a shield is an expression for their preparing and readying them for the time of need, so that they might swear by them and be freed from punishment, not for actually using them, since that comes after the punishment, which is preceded by the commission of the offence, whereas taking a shield must occur before the punishment. It is also an expression for the cause of it, as the fa' in ﴿fa-saddu﴾ (so they barred) makes clear, that is, whoever wished to embrace Islam or to spend [in God's cause], as will be related about them. There is no doubt that this barring precedes their oath. It is read by al-Hasan as "imanahum" (their faith) with a kasrah on the hamzah, meaning what they manifested on their tongues. Then taking it as a shield is an expression for its actual use, since it protects them, but not their blood and property. The meaning of God's words ﴿so they barred﴾ is: so they persisted in what they had been upon of turning away and averting from His way, may He be exalted. End of quotation. In it is what becomes clear upon reflection, so reflect.

﴿Indeed, evil is what they used to do﴾, namely hypocrisy and what follows from it. The discussion of "evil" (sa'a) has already passed more than once.

[Page 110]

﴿That﴾ refers to what was mentioned earlier, the statement condemning them as the worst of people in their deeds. It may also refer to their condition of hypocrisy, lying, and hiding behind false oaths or a merely outward faith. The demonstrative carries a sense of distance, though the referent is close in the text, and as has been noted many times before in such contexts, this implies how far their rank is in evil. Ibn 'Atiyya permitted that it refers to the evil of what they did, so the meaning would be: ﴿evil is their deed﴾. ﴿Because﴾, meaning on account of the fact that ﴿they﴾ ﴿believed﴾, that is, they uttered the testimony of faith as all who enter Islam do, ﴿then disbelieved﴾. Their disbelief became apparent and was made clear by what was discovered of their words: "If what Muhammad says is true, then we are donkeys," and their saying during the expedition of Tabuk: "Does this man hope that the palaces of Kisra and Caesar will be opened to him? Far-fetched!" and other such things. The ﴿then﴾ (thumma) is in its literal sense, or it expresses the improbability of the gap between the two states. Or the sense is: they concealed disbelief, and thumma here is only for emphasizing improbability. Or: they professed faith in front of the believers, then professed disbelief in front of their devils, mocking Islam. It has also been said that the verse concerns those among them who apostatized (al-Ridda, apostasy).

﴿So a seal was set upon their hearts﴾, until they die in disbelief, ﴿so they do not understand﴾ the reality of faith at all.

Zayd ibn 'Ali recited "فَطَبَعَ" in the active voice, with its subject being the pronoun of Him, the Exalted. It has been permitted that the pronoun refers to the verbal noun understood from what precedes it, meaning: "so it (the mockery) sealed," that is, their playing with religion. In one report he recited "فَطَبَعَ اللَّهُ" explicitly naming God, the Majestic. Al-A'mash also recited it in the same way.

[Page 111]

﴿And when you see them, their bodies please you﴾ because of their handsome appearance and the proportion of their limbs. ﴿And if they speak, you listen to what they say﴾ because of their eloquence, the fluency of their tongues, and the sweetness of their speech. Ibn Ubayy was a large, eloquent man who attended the gathering of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) along with a group of his like, such as al-Jadd ibn Qays and Mut'ib ibn Qushayr. Thus the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and those with him would marvel at their physical forms and listen to their speech. It has been said that the address is to everyone fit to receive it. This is supported by the reading of ʿIkrima and ʿAṭiyya al-ʿAwfī, "yusmaʿ" (with a ya' and in the passive voice). It has also been said that the address is to the chief of those addressed, peace be upon him, and this is more eloquent according to what is in al-Kashf (al-Zamakhshari's commentary), because if their bodies pleased him (may God's peace and blessings be upon him), then they are all the more likely to please others. The same applies to listening to their speech. It also accords with God's words ﴿when they come to you﴾. Listening is implicitly equivalent in meaning to giving ear, so the lam is not superfluous.

God's words ﴿as if they were propped-up timber﴾ are a new sentence serving to censure them, and it has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis). It has been allowed that it may be in the nominative position, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "They are as if they were..." etc., and this sentence is also new. You know that the sentence is fit to stand as a new sentence without any estimation, so there is no need for that. It has also been said that it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿for their speech﴾, meaning: "You listen to what they say, likened to propped-up timber," as in the verse:

*"I said, perhaps you will see me, as if the fierce lions were built around me."*

It has been objected that a circumstantial clause implies that listening to their speech is because they are like propped-up timber, and that is not the case. The word "khushub" is the plural of "khashaba," like "thamara" and "thumur." What is meant is the well-known thing. They were likened, in their sitting in the gatherings of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) leaning in them, to lifeless bodies devoid of faith and goodness, to timber set up and propped against a wall, in being shapes devoid of benefit, because timber is propped only when it is not part of a building or supported by something else. It has also been allowed that by "propped-up timber" is meant idols carved from timber propped against walls, and they were likened to these in the beauty of their forms and the scarcity of their benefit. Concerning such people the poet said:

*"Do not let beards or appearances deceive you; nine-tenths of those you see are cattle."*

*"You see them like clouds spread out, but there is no rain in them for the seeker."*

*"Among them is a resemblance to a cypress tree, which has a fine appearance but no fruit."*

Al-Bara' ibn ʿAzib, the two grammarians (al-Kisa'i and Hamza), and Ibn Kathir read "khushb" with a sukun on the shin, as a lightened form of "khushub" with a damma, like "badana" and "budn." It has also been said that it is the plural of "khashbā'," like "ḥumr" and "ḥamrā'," and this is the piece of timber whose inside has been hollowed out. They were likened to it in the corruption of their inner states because of their hypocrisy. It is reported from al-Yazidi that he interpreted the majority reading with a damma in this way, but it has been objected that "fa'lā'" is not pluralized as "fu'ul" with two dammas, and from this the weakness of that opinion is known, since the basic principle is agreement among the readings.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Musayyab, and Ibn Jubayr read "khashab" with two fathas, like "madra" and "madar," and it is a noun of genus according to what is in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit). Its description is in the feminine, as in God's words ﴿as if they were hollow palm trunks﴾ [al-Haqqah 7]. ﴿They think every shout is against them﴾, meaning, falling upon them, harmful to them, because of their cowardice and panic. Thus, as Muqatil said, whenever they heard the announcement of a lost animal, or a shout in any way, their minds flew away and they thought it was an attack upon them. It has also been said that they were in dread lest God, mighty and majestic, should send down concerning them something that would tear away their veils and make lawful their blood and property. From this sense Jarir took his words addressing al-Akhtal:

*"You have always thought that after them every thing was horsemen charging upon them, and men."*

Likewise al-Mutanabbi said:

*"The earth became so narrow that the fleeing one among them thought, whenever he saw something other than himself, that it was a man."*

Stopping at "ʿalayhim" [upon them], which is the second object of "yaḥsabūn," is a complete pause, as in al-Kawashi, and al-Wahidi's words accord with this.

God's words ﴿They are the enemy﴾ are a new sentence, meaning: they are the complete and firmly established in enmity. For the worst of enemies is the deceitful enemy who flatters you while under his ribs is a deadly disease, like many of the sons of the age. ﴿So beware of them﴾, because they are the worst of enemies, and do not be deceived by their outward appearance. Al-Zamakhshari allowed that ﴿upon them﴾ could be the complement of "ṣayḥa" [shout], and ﴿they are the enemy﴾ could be the second object of "yaḥsabūn," as if the pronoun were omitted, meaning that they think the shout itself is the enemy. The apparent form would then be "huwa" or "hiya" [he or she is] the enemy, but he used the pronoun for rational plural to observe the meaning of the predicate, namely "the enemy," on the basis that it may be both plural and singular, and here it is plural. But this is a strained and very distant interpretation, not needed, though the meaning is not without eloquence and subtlety in it. Even so, the sequence of ﴿so beware of them﴾ does not support it, because warning against them requires describing them as enemies, not as cowards.

﴿May God destroy them﴾, meaning, may He curse and expel them. For killing is the utmost of the hardships and horrors of this world. Likewise, being expelled from God's mercy and distanced from His most holy presence is the furthest end of His punishment, mighty and majestic, and the ultimate of His retribution, exalted, in this world and the next. The statement is a supplication and a request from Him, glorified, that He curse them and expel them from His mercy, exalted. This is from the style of tajrid (abstraction, where the speaker addresses himself or another as if separate), so it is not the placing of an apparent noun in place of a pronoun, because by that the freshness of the speech would be lost. Or it is an instruction to the believers that they should invoke this upon them, so the meaning is: "Say: May God destroy them." It has also been allowed that it is not a request at all, but that the occurrence of the curse upon them is established and unavoidable. Some have mentioned that "qātalahu Allāh" is a word of censure and rebuke, and the Arabs use it in the place of wonder without intending a curse. The well-known usage is to follow it with wonder, as in "qātalahu Allāh, mā ash'arahu" [God destroy him, how knowing he is!]. Likewise God's words here, glorified: ﴿May God destroy them﴾.

﴿How are they turned away?﴾ This is an expression of wonder at their condition, meaning: how are they turned away from the truth to what they are upon of disbelief and error? So "annā" is an adverb containing the sense of interrogation, governing what follows it. Ibn ʿAṭiyya allowed that it may be an adverb governed by "qātalahum," and there is no interrogation there. Abu Hayyan objected to him, saying that "annā" never has merely the sense of place at all, so that opinion is false.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 63, verse 5:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Come, the Messenger of Allah will seek forgiveness for you," they turn their heads aside.﴾ Meaning: they bend them (ʿaṭafūhā). This is a metaphor (kināya) for arrogance and aversion, according to what has been said. It was also said that it is in its literal sense, i.e., they shook them in mockery. Ibn al-Mundhir related it from Ibn Jurayj. ﴿And you see them turning away﴾ — they turn away from the speaker or from seeking forgiveness, ﴿while they are arrogant﴾ — from that.

It is narrated that when Allah confirmed Zayd ibn Arqam in what he reported about Ibn Ubayy, the people despised Ibn Ubayy, and the believers of his people blamed him. Some of them said to him: "Go to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, admit your sin, and he will seek forgiveness for you." So he turned his head, rejecting this opinion, and said to them: "You have advised me to believe, so I believed; you advised me to give the zakat of my wealth, so I did it. Nothing remains for you but to order me to prostrate to Muhammad ﷺ."

In a hadith related by ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Abi Ḥatim from Ibn Jubayr: that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him, "Repent," so he began to turn his head, and Allah revealed ﴿And when it is said to them﴾ etc.

In a hadith related by Imam Aḥmad, al-Shaykhān, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and others from Zayd, after recounting the story, he said: "Until Allah revealed my confirmation in ﴿When the hypocrites come to you﴾, whose text is: so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called them that he might seek forgiveness for them, and they turned their heads."

As for the plural of the pronouns: either it is on its apparent sense, or it is of the type of "Banu Tamim killed so-and-so." And ﴿idhā﴾ is as mentioned above. ﴿Yastaghfir﴾ is jussive as an answer to the imperative, and ﴿Rasulu Allah﴾ is its subject (fāʿil). The construction, according to what is in al-Bahr, is of the type of iʿmāl (government of two verbs over one noun), because ﴿Rasulu Allah﴾ is sought by two governing verbs: ﴿yastaghfir﴾ and ﴿taʿālaw﴾. The second was made to govern, according to the preferred view of the Basrans. Had the first been made to govern, the construction would have been "taʿālaw yustaghfar lakum ilā Rasuli Allah." The clause ﴿yaṣudduna﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and it uses the present tense to indicate continuous, renewed occurrence. Similar in circumstantial function is the clause ﴿wa-hum mustakbirūn﴾. Mujahid, Nafi', the people of Medina, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, al-Mufaddal, Aban from ʿAsim, al-Hasan and Yaʿqub (with a variant from them both) read ﴿lawwaw﴾ with the letter waw lightened, while the doubling (tashdīd) in the reading of the rest of the seven is for intensification.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 63, verse 6:

When Allah (glorified is He) censured them for their refusal to come so that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would ask forgiveness for them, and for their turning away and arrogance, He (mighty and majestic) indicated the uselessness of seeking forgiveness for them, because He knew of the badness of their preparedness and their choice, by His saying (exalted is He): ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾. This is for equating the two matters, seeking forgiveness for them and not seeking it, and the intended meaning is the information that there is no benefit, as His saying (mighty and majestic is His state) reveals: ﴿Allah will never forgive them﴾. Its reason, in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the defiant people﴾, meaning those who are complete in defiance, outside the circle of reform, plunged into every kind of vileness because of the badness of their preparedness. For forgiveness is a branch of guidance. The "people" here may be those spoken of by their individual persons. The explicit noun in place of the pronoun is to show their extremeness in defiance, and to point to the cause of the ruling. Or it is the category, and they are included in it by primary inclusion. The verse, concerning Ibn Ubayy, is like its predecessors, as you have heard, and its successors, as is established, and you will hear it soon, if Allah (exalted is He) wills. As for seeking forgiveness for them, it has been said: on the condition that they come repentant and apologizing for their offenses. This had been taken into account in the matter whose answer was jussive (the verb), since otherwise mere coming does not appear to be a cause for seeking forgiveness. This is hinted at by the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to Ibn Ubayy in the report of Ibn Jubayr: "Repent." Leaving off seeking forgiveness is on the condition of persistence in vileness and arrogance and not apologizing. And since there was no repentance from them, the Messenger (peace be upon him) did not seek forgiveness for them.

Makki narrated that he (ﷺ) did seek forgiveness for them, because they showed him Islam, meaning after what had proceeded from them, with repentance. Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When the verse of Bara'a, ﴿Seek forgiveness for them or do not seek forgiveness for them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 80], etc., was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "My Lord has granted me leave concerning them. By Allah, I will seek forgiveness for them more than seventy times, perhaps Allah will forgive them." Then this verse was revealed: ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾, etc.

He also reported similar from 'Urwah. If this is established, it is not possible to say that the whole of Bara'a was the last thing revealed, and there is no necessity compelling one to hold to it, unless a transmission is established that does not admit of interpretation. Perhaps this verse is an indication from Him (exalted is He) to His Prophet (ﷺ) that the intended meaning of the number there is multiplicity, not specific limitation, so that the ruling of the excess would differ from the ruling of what was mentioned. Thus the intended meaning of the two verses with Allah (exalted is He) is one, namely the absence of forgiveness for them absolutely. The first verse, in my choice, was revealed concerning those who defame, as you heard there from Ibn 'Abbas, and this is more suitable to the context. This one was revealed concerning Ibn Ubayy and his companions, as the sound reports have spoken. What unites the two groups is hypocrisy, and for this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said what he said, despite the difference in the individuals about whom the two were revealed. Furthermore, I have not found in anything I rely upon that Ibn Ubayy was ill at that time. I saw in a report that 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn Sirin something indicating that after his saying, "By Allah, if we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it," after a few days he fell ill and his pain intensified. In it, he said to the Prophet (ﷺ), when he came to him seeking intercession through his son: "My need, if I die, is that you witness my washing, shroud me in three garments from your garments, walk with my funeral procession, and pray over me." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did this, and then the verse was revealed: ﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever, nor stand at his grave﴾ [al-Tawbah: 84]. There is no difficulty in seeking forgiveness, if it occurred for one of the hypocrites after the revelation of what indicates that He (exalted is He) does not guide the defiant people, since it is not determined that each of them is included except by clarifying that he specifically is among the companions of the Hellfire, such as dying in what he was upon of disbelief and hypocrisy. What I have mentioned here is what became clear to me after writing what I wrote on the verse of Bara'a, and the matter still needs verification, so review and reflect. And Allah (exalted is He) is the Granter of success.

Abu Ja'far read "ءَسْتَغْفَرْتَ" with a madda on the hamza. It was said: it is a substitute for the hamza of wasl, and it is like the madda in His saying (exalted is He): "Say: Is it the two males He has forbidden?" [al-An'am: 143, 144]. But this madda in the noun is so that the interrogative is not confused with the declarative, and this is not needed in the verb, because the hamza of wasl in it is kasra. Also from him: the damma of the mim in "'alayhimu," since its original is damma with the joining of the hamza. Mu'adh ibn Mu'adh al-'Anbari narrated from Abu 'Amr the kasra of the mim, on the basis of the meeting of two sukuns, and the joining of the hamza, so it drops in both readings, and the wording is declarative while the meaning is interrogative. The omission of the hamza came trusting in the indication of "am" upon it, as in the saying of the poet:

"Bi-sab'in ramayna al-jamra am bi-thamanin"

Al-Zamakhshari said: Abu Ja'far read "ءاسْتَغْفَرْتَ" with elongation of the interrogative hamza for clarity and explanation, not by changing the hamza of wasl into an alif as in "ءالسِّحْرِ" and "ءاللَّهِ." Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' said: with a madda on the hamza, and it is the alif of equalization.

He also read with wasl of the alif without a hamza, on the declarative. In that there is weakness, because in the first he affirmed the hamza of wasl although the interrogative hamza has already sufficed for it, and in the second he dropped the interrogative hamza while intending it, and this is something that is only used in poetry.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 63, verse 7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They are the ones who say, "Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse."﴾ is a resumptive statement (istinaf) explaining some of what indicates their wickedness (fisq). It has been permitted that it be taken as serving as a cause (ta'lil) for His not forgiving them, exalted is He, but this is not correct, because that is explained by what precedes it. The one who said it was the head of the hypocrites, Ibn Ubayy, and the rest of them were content with that. al-Tirmidhi narrated it and authenticated it, as did a group, from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: "We went on a military expedition (ghazwa) with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and with us were some Bedouins (a'rab). We would race to the water, and the Bedouins would get ahead of us to it. A Bedouin would get ahead of his companions, fill the basin, make his basin of stones, and place the leather mat (nit') over it until his companions came. A man from the Ansar came upon a Bedouin and loosened the rein of his she-camel so that it might drink, but the Bedouin refused to let him, so he pulled out a stone, and the water poured out. The Bedouin raised a piece of wood and struck the Ansari's head, wounding him. Then 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, the head of the hypocrites, who was one of his companions, came and was informed, and he became angry and said: ﴿Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse﴾ from around him, meaning the Bedouins. Then he said to his companions: 'When you return to Medina, the mightier (al-a'azz) among them will drive out the meaner (al-adhall).' Zayd said: 'I was riding behind my uncle, and I heard 'Abd Allah, so I informed my uncle, and he informed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The Messenger of Allah sent for him, and he swore and denied it, and the Messenger ﷺ believed him and called me a liar. My uncle came to me and said: "I did not intend anything except that the Messenger of Allah hated you and the Muslims called you a liar." So grief came upon me such as had never befallen anyone. While I was walking with my head bowed from grief, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to me, pulled my ear, and smiled in my face. Then Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, caught up with me and said: "What did the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say to you?" I said: "He said nothing to me except that he pulled my ear and smiled in my face." He said: "Rejoice." When we rose in the morning, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited ﴿When the hypocrites come to you, they say, "We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah"﴾ until he reached ﴿The mightier among them will surely drive out the meaner.﴾"

And what has preceded from al-Bukhari indicates that he also said that. Imam Ahmad, Muslim and al-Nasa'i narrated something similar, and the reports on this are more than can be counted. As for that expedition to which Zayd referred, Sufyan said: they hold that it was the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq. In the Kashshaf there is a lengthy report about the incident, from which it is understood that by "those who are with the Messenger of Allah" they meant the poor Emigrants (fuqara' al-muhajirin). The apparent reading is that the expression "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ" — that is, with this exact wording — came from them, and their disbelief does not preclude it, because they were hypocrites who outwardly acknowledged his prophethood, peace be upon him.

It has been permitted that they said it mockingly (tahakkuman), or because of his being so overwhelmingly known by it, peace be upon him, until it became like a proper name (ka-l-'alam), with no intention in it except the person. It is also possible that they expressed it with other wording, and Allah, mighty and majestic, changed it out of honour and esteem for His Prophet, peace be upon him.

Al-infidad means dispersal (al-tafarruq). And "until" (hatta) here indicates cause (lil-ta'lil), meaning: do not spend on them so that they will disperse from him, peace be upon him, and not accompany him.

al-Fadl ibn 'Isa al-Raqqashi read yanfudu (with the verb from anfada), meaning: the people's food ran out (anfada al-qawm, faniya ta'amuhum), so the man shook out his provision bag (nafada al-rajulu wi'a'ahu). The verb is transitive without the hamza and intransitive with it. In the Kashshaf he said: its literal meaning is that it became time for them to shake out their saddlebags (mazawid).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to Allah belong the treasuries of the heavens and the earth﴾ is a refutation and nullification of what they claimed, that their not spending on those who are with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would lead to their dispersal from him, peace be upon him, by making clear that the treasuries of provision are in the hand of Allah alone; He gives from them to whom He wills and withholds from whom He wills. ﴿But the hypocrites do not understand﴾ this, because of their ignorance of Allah, exalted is He, and of His affairs, mighty and majestic; and for this reason they say of the sayings of the disbelievers what they say.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 63, verse 8:

﴿They say: "If we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it."﴾ The speaker, as you have heard, is Ibn Ubayy. By "the mightier" he meant himself or those who take refuge with him, and by "the meaner" he meant the one whom Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has made mighty, namely the Messenger (ﷺ), or, as another view holds, the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers. The statement is attributed to all of them because they were content with it, as in the preceding verse.

Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ablah and al-Sabti, in his own selection, read «لَنُخْرِجَنَّ» with the nun, and «الأعَزَّ» and «الأذَلَّ» in the accusative. Here «الأعَزَّ» is the direct object. As for «الأذَلَّ», it may be a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, a state of the subject or object) on the basis that a ḥāl may be definite, or the alif-lam in it is extra, as in the phrase «أرْسَلَها العِراكَ» (he sent it running freely), and «ادْخُلُوا الأوَّلَ فالأوَّلَ» (enter one after another). This is the best-known explanation of such forms. It may also be a ḥāl with an implied «مِثْلٍ» (like), since that word is not made definite by its genitive construction, so the sense is "like the meaner." It may be a maf'ul bihi (direct object) of an implied ḥāl, meaning "resembling the meaner." Or it may be a maf'ul mutlaq (absolute object, cognate accusative), on the basis that the original sense is "the expulsion of the meaner," then the verbal noun was omitted, the genitive noun was put in its place, and it took the same accusative case.

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' related that some people read «لَيَخْرُجُنَّ» with a fatḥah on the yā' and a ḍammah on the rā', with «الأعَزُّ» in the nominative as subject (fā'il), and «الأذَلَّ» in the accusative as explained above. However, if you take the accusative as a verbal noun, you must supply «خُرُوجٌ» (departure) as its implied verb noun. It was also read «لَيُخْرَجَنَّ» with the yā' and in the passive voice, with «الأعَزُّ» in the nominative as deputy subject (nā'ib al-fā'il), and «الأذَلَّ» in the accusative as explained earlier.

Al-Hasan, as reported by Abu Amr al-Dani, read «لَنَخْرُجَنَّ» with the nun of the plural, a fatḥah, and a ḍammah on the rā', with «الأعَزَّ» and «الأذَلَّ» in the accusative. Abu Hatim also related this reading. It is explained as follows: the accusative of «الأعَزَّ» is one of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ, a noun put in the accusative to single out a group), as in the saying "We, the Arabs, are the most hospitable of people to a guest." The accusative of «الأذَلَّ» is one of the possibilities mentioned above that al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' related. The purpose is to express the believers' impatience with them, and the claim that they could not live with them in the same abode. This is what has been said, but it is as you see. Perhaps this reading is not reliably reported from al-Hasan.

Allah's words ﴿And might belongs to Allah, to His Messenger and to the believers﴾ are a rebuttal of what they implicitly claimed about their own might and the humiliation of the one they attributed humiliation to, far be it from him. The meaning is: to Allah, Exalted, belong dominance and power, and to the one whom Allah has made mighty among His Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers, and not to anyone else. From what we have indicated, the restriction (ḥaṣr) derived from placing the predicate first becomes clear. It has been said that the conjunction is intended before the attribution, so that this does not conflict with it, and repeating the preposition does no harm, because it is not meant to make the attribution independent, but rather to show the difference in the establishment of might. Its establishment for Allah, Exalted, is essential, for the Messenger (ﷺ) it is through the mission, and for the believers it is through faith.

It has come by several chains that ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy, who was sincere, drew his sword against his father when they approached Medina, and said: "By Allah, I will not sheathe it until you say that Muhammad is the mightier and I am the meaner." He did not leave off until he said it. In another report, he (may Allah be pleased with him) stood at the gate while people were entering, until his father came and said: "Stay behind you." He said: "What is wrong with you, woe to you?" He said: "By Allah, you will never enter it unless the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gives permission, and today you will know who is the mightier and who is the meaner." So he returned until he met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and complained to him of what his son had done. The Prophet (ﷺ) sent to him: "Let him go, so that he may enter." He did so.

It is authentic, from the narrations of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), al-Tirmidhi and others, from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) received what Ibn Ubayy had said, ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) stood up and said: "O Messenger of Allah, let me strike the neck of this hypocrite." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Leave him, so that people do not say that Muhammad kills his companions." In a report from Qatada, he said to him (peace and blessings be upon him): "O Prophet of Allah, order Muʿadh to strike the neck of this hypocrite," and the Prophet (ﷺ) said that.

The verse contains evidence of the nobility of the believers, and for this reason some righteous women, who were in ragged clothing, said: "Am I not upon Islam? It is the might that has no humiliation with it, and the wealth that has no poverty with it."

It is related from al-Hasan ibn ʿAli, upon the Messenger of Allah and upon both of them be peace and blessings, that a man said to him: "People claim that there is arrogance (tīh) in you." He said: "It is not arrogance, but it is might (ʿizzah)," and he recited this verse. Here "tīh" means pride, and the words "might" indicate that might is other than pride. Abu Hafs al-Suhrawardi (may Allah sanctify his secret) explicitly stated this, saying: "Might is other than pride, because might is a person's knowledge of the reality of his own self, and honouring it means not placing it in lowly matters, just as pride is a person's ignorance of himself and placing himself above his station. Thus might is the opposite of humiliation, just as pride is the opposite of humility."

Al-Raghib explained might as a condition that prevents a person from being overcome, from their saying "a firm land" (arḍ ʿazzāz), meaning hard, and "the flesh became firm" (taʿazzaza al-laḥm), meaning it became hard, as if it had come into a hard place that is difficult to reach. It may also be used metaphorically for zealous and blameworthy pride, and in this sense it applies to the unbelievers. Explaining it as power and dominance, as you have heard, is common. You may also intend by it here the condition that prevents being overcome, for this is also established for Allah, Exalted, for His Messenger (ﷺ) and for the believers, in the manner appropriate to each.

﴿But the hypocrites do not know﴾ because of their extreme ignorance and deception, so they utter what they utter. The verb here is treated as intransitive, so no object is supposed for it, unlike the verb in the previous statement. This is what many eminent scholars have chosen. It has been said regarding its reason: the fact that might belongs to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, entails that provisions are in His hand, but not the converse. Therefore it was appropriate to mention the mention of morals in the clause that follows, which indicates that might belongs to Him, Glorified, intentionally for emphasis. The restriction in the clause that follows, which indicates that provisions are in the hand of Allah, Exalted, is also relevant. Then it has been said: the first clause is specified by ﴿do not understand﴾ and the second by ﴿do not know﴾, because affirming understanding (fiqh) for a person is more eloquent than affirming knowledge for him. Therefore the negation of knowledge is more eloquent than the negation of understanding, so the more eloquent was placed at the end, as it is more fitting for it.

Al-Raghib explained the meaning of Allah's words ﴿They are those who say: "Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah"﴾ etc. as meaning that they command harm to the believers and the withholding of expenses from them, and they do not realise that if they do this they harm themselves. Thus they do not understand this and are not aware of it. The meaning of the second is their threat to expel the mightier for the meaner. In their view, the mightier is the one who has power and dominance, as they were in the days of ignorance. They do not know that this power by which a person surpasses others is from Allah, Exalted. Therefore it belongs to Him, Glorified, and to whomever He singles out for it among His servants. They also do not know that humiliation belongs to those whom they assume to have might, and that Allah, Exalted, makes His friends mighty through their obedience to Him, and humiliates His enemies through their opposition to His command, Mighty and Majestic. Thus each verse has been specified by what its meaning requires, so reflect upon it. The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun serves to intensify the reproach, together with an indication of the cause of the ruling in both places.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 63, verse 9:

﴿O you who have believed, let not your wealth or your children divert you from the remembrance of Allah.﴾ That is: let not your preoccupation with managing their affairs, caring for their interests, and enjoying them distract you from occupying yourselves with the remembrance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, namely the prayer and the other acts of worship mentioned for the true God, exalted is His majesty. Thus the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted, is a metaphor (majaz) for worship in general, as the statement of al-Hasan and a group of scholars implies, and the relationship (ʿalaqah) is causal, because worship is a cause of remembering Him, glorified is He, and that remembrance is in reality the purpose of it.

It is related from al-Hasan that what is meant by it is all the obligatory duties (al-fara'id). al-Dahhak and ʿAtaʾ said: the remembrance here is the prescribed prayer (al-salat al-maktubah). al-Kalbi said: it is jihad alongside the Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. It was also said: it is the Qur'an. The generality is more appropriate. The statement of al-Kashshaf implies that what is meant by wealth and children is the worldly life, and he expressed it through these two because they are the most desired of things in it. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world﴾ [al-Kahf: 46]. So when the remembrance of Allah is taken in its general sense, the meaning reverts to: let not the world distract you from the religion. The prohibition in "wealth and what follows it" is directed at the addressees, and it was directed at those things only for emphasis, because they are the strongest cause of heedlessness and have the greatest influence in it; so they were made as though they themselves were heedless, while the prohibition is in fact upon the people. The original sense is: do not be heedless through your wealth, and so on. The figure lies in the attribution (al-tajawwuz fi al-isnad). It was also said that it is a metonymy of the cause for the effect (tajawwuz bi al-sabab ʿan al-musabbab), like His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿So let there be no constriction in your breast﴾ [al-A'raf: 2], meaning: do not be in a state where your wealth diverts you, and so on.

﴿And whoever does that﴾, that is, makes heedless through them, which is preoccupation, and this is more eloquent than if it had been said: "and whoever is diverted by those." ﴿Then those are the losers﴾, in that they have sold the great and enduring for the small and perishing. In the definition by the demonstrative and in the restriction (hasr) of loss to them, and in the repetition of the attribution and the insertion of the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl), there is emphasis that is not hidden. And it seems that when the hypocrites were forbidden from spending on those who are with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and encouragement to spend was intended, His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿O you who have believed﴾, and so on, was made a preface and a preparation for the command to spend, but in a general manner in His statement, glorified is He:

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 63, verse 10:**

﴿And spend from what We have provided you﴾, i.e., some of what We have given you and bestowed upon you of wealth, as a store for the Hereafter, ﴿before death comes to one of you﴾, i.e., its signs and precursors. The statement therefore contains an elided noun (mudaf, a noun in annexation), which is why He follows it with His words: ﴿Then he says, "My Lord, if only You would delay me﴾, i.e., grant me respite, ﴿for a short term﴾, i.e., a brief period, ﴿so I would give charity [fa-assaddaqa]﴾, i.e., so I would give charity (fa-atasaddaqa). Ubayy, Abd Allah and Ibn Jubayr read it this way. The verb is in the subjunctive as the answer to the wish (tamanni). The jussive in His words, glorified is He: ﴿and be among the righteous﴾, is by coordination (ʿatf) with the position (mawdiʿ) of fa-assaddaqa, as if it were said: "If You delay me, I will give charity and be [among the righteous]." This is the view of Abu Ali al-Farisi and al-Zajjaj. Sibawayh reported from al-Khalil that it is on the basis of an assumed conditional (tawahhum al-shart), which the wish implies, because the condition is not apparent and is not assumed so as to justify coordination with the position, as in His words: ﴿Whomever God leads astray, there is no guide for him﴾ [al-A'raf: 186], and [as in] ﴿and leaves them﴾ for those who read it with the jussive. It is good, but expressing it through tawahhum here gives rise to an ugly notion. The difference between coordination with the position (al-ʿatf ʿala al-mawdiʿ) and coordination with the assumed (al-ʿatf ʿala al-tawahhum) is that the governing element in the first exists while its effect is absent, whereas the governing element in the second is absent while its effect exists. It has been inferred that the disagreement is merely verbal, since what Abu Ali and al-Zajjaj mean is coordination with the assumed or estimated position, that is, the presumed one, for there is in reality no position here, but they both avoided the ugliness of the expression.

Al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Abu Raja, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Malik ibn Dinar, al-A'mash, Ibn Muhaysin and Abd Allah ibn al-Hasan al-Anbari read [the verse with] "wa-akun" (and I would be). Abu Amr read "wa-akuna" with the accusative, which is clear. Abd ibn Umayr read "wa-akunu" with the nominative, as a resumption (isti'naf). The grammarians and the scholars of meaning (ahl al-ma'ani) estimate an implied subject (mubtada') in such resumed verbal clauses, so it is said here: "That is, wa-ana akunu" (and I would be). You do not find them neglecting this. It has been justified on the ground that the verb is not suitable for resumption with the resumptive "wa" as here, nor without it. It has been objected that no grammarian has held that it is unsuitable for this, and it is for this reason that the scholar al-Taftazani explicitly stated that the necessity of positing an estimate is something whose justification he has not seen. It has been said that its justification is that resumption with a nominal clause is more apparent, and this, as you see, is weak. It is also permitted that the verb in this reading be nominative by coordination with "assaddaqu," in the manner of the two views mentioned above regarding the jussive.

Further, al-Dahhak said regarding His words: ﴿Spend of what We have provided you﴾, that it means zakat and expenditure for the pilgrimage (Hajj). Ibn Abbas's statement is also in this sense, as reported by Ibn al-Mundhir: "fa-assaddaqa" means "I would pay zakat" and "wa-akun min al-salihin" means "I would perform Hajj." Al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani and others also reported from him that he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has wealth that enables him to reach the House of his Lord [for Hajj], or on which zakat is due, and does not do it, will ask to be returned at death." A man said to him: "O Ibn Abbas, fear God, for only the disbelievers ask to be returned." He said: "I will recite to you a Qur'an on this: ﴿O you who have believed, let not your wealth or your children divert you from the remembrance of God﴾," to the end of the surah. Thus [it is reported] in al-Durr al-Manthur.

In Ahkam al-Qur'an, there is al-Tirmidhi's narration from him of this as a mawquf (halted at his level, not traced to the Prophet). It is also related from him in al-Bahr and elsewhere that he said: "This verse was revealed concerning one who withholds zakat. By God, if he had seen goodness, he would not have asked to be returned." It was said to him: "Do you not fear God? Do the believers ask for a return?" He then answered with something similar to what has been mentioned. It is not hidden that the objection to him, and likewise the answer, is more fitting if he himself claimed that the request for a return was made, and did not attribute the hadith to this. And if His words, ﴿if only You would delay me﴾ and so on, are a request for return (raj'ah) in the sense of returning to the world after death, then His words ﴿before death comes to one of you﴾ do not require positing an elided noun, as you have just seen.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 63, verse 11:

﴿And Allah will never delay a soul﴾, i.e., will never grant it respite, ﴿when its term comes﴾, i.e., the last of its lifespan, or the time extending for it from the beginning of its life to its end, according to interpreting the term (ajal) in this way. ﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do﴾, so He will recompense you for it. Abu Bakr read it with the letter ya' (third person), to agree with what precedes it in the third person. And "nafsan" (a soul), because it is indefinite in the context of negation, has the sense of plurality. Al-Kiya (Ilkiya al-Harrasi) argued, from the words of the Exalted, ﴿And spend﴾ etc., for the obligation of paying zakat (obligatory alms) immediately and the prohibition of delaying it. It is attributed to al-Zamakhshari that he said: "There is nothing more severe than this in warning against neglecting these rights. No one delays it without it being possible that death comes upon him soon, so he must be extremely careful against this neglect at all times." Allah the Exalted has refuted the view of the Mujabbira (Jabriyya, the determinists) in several ways. Among them is the Exalted's words ﴿And spend﴾. Among them is that before the arrival of death, he was not able to spend, so how could he wish for the delay of the term? Among them is the Exalted's words, encouraging him to despair in the answer: ﴿And Allah will never delay﴾. Had He not been one who chooses, the answer would have been the equality of delay and death at the time of the wish. It has been answered that the People of Truth (Ahl al-Haqq) do not hold the doctrine of compulsion (jabr), so the argument falls away from them. Moreover, there is no proof in the first (verse) as in all other commands, as has been verified in its proper place. And the wish, which is the basis of the group, cannot be validly used as evidence. The statement that brings despair is a refutation of their wish and has no answer against it, since clear falsehood does not deserve a reply. And Allah the Exalted knows best.
